questions.statement: Which opening is appropriate for a formal email to a school principal?
questions.context: A student must write to a school principal to request a change of class.

options.text: Dear Mr Sanchez,
options.feedback: Correct! 'Dear' plus a title and a surname is the standard formal opening in English.

options.text: Hey Sam,
options.feedback: 'Hey' is an informal greeting used between friends.

options.text: Hi there,
options.feedback: 'Hi there' is a casual greeting that does not suit a formal exchange.

options.text: Hello friend,
options.feedback: 'Hello friend' states a relationship that a principal letter does not have.

questions.explanation:
The opening line sets the register of the whole message. A title and a surname with 'dear' is the convention for formal English correspondence.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which closing is appropriate for a formal email to a school principal?
questions.context: A student finishes an email addressed by name to the head of a school.

options.text: Bye for now,
options.feedback: 'Bye for now' is a casual farewell between peers.

options.text: Yours sincerely,
options.feedback: Correct! 'Yours sincerely' is the standard formal closing when the recipient is named.

options.text: See you later,
options.feedback: 'See you later' implies a future meeting and is informal.

options.text: Love,
options.feedback: 'Love' expresses affection and does not belong in formal correspondence.

questions.explanation:
English uses paired conventions: 'dear' plus a name takes 'yours sincerely', while a formal opening without a name takes 'yours faithfully'.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which subject line is most appropriate for an email requesting a change of class?
questions.context: A student writes an email about a class change and must fill in the subject field.

options.text: Hello
options.feedback: 'Hello' is a greeting and not a subject.

options.text: Something important
options.feedback: 'Something important' is vague and gives the reader no idea of the content.

options.text: Request for a change of class
options.feedback: Correct! The subject states the topic precisely and lets the reader identify the email at a glance.

options.text: Question about stuff
options.feedback: 'Question about stuff' is informal and imprecise in both content and tone.

questions.explanation:
The subject line is a summary in a few words. It is the first thing the reader sees and it decides whether the message is opened.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence is the most formal way to begin the body of a request?
questions.context: A student addresses a request to an authority figure in writing.

options.text: I want to change class, can I?
options.feedback: The first sentence is a direct question that is too blunt for a request to a superior.

options.text: Hey, so I need a new class, you know.
options.feedback: The second sentence is spoken register and does not belong in a formal email.

options.text: I am telling you that I am asking about a class.
options.feedback: The third sentence is verbose without adding information, and it states nothing about the request.

options.text: I am writing to ask whether it would be possible to transfer to another class.
options.feedback: Correct! 'I am writing to ask whether' is a conventional and appropriately indirect opening for a formal request.

questions.explanation:
Formal English softens a request with hedged verbs and indirect wording. The politeness is grammatical, not merely a matter of politeness words.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which modal is most appropriate in a formal request?
questions.context: A student asks a school to authorise something and must phrase the ask politely.

options.text: It would be possible to
options.feedback: Correct! 'Would be' is a hedged construction that leaves the decision with the recipient.

options.text: You must do it
options.feedback: 'You must' imposes an obligation and is not a request.

options.text: You have to do it now
options.feedback: 'You have to' also imposes an obligation and is too direct in this context.

options.text: It is a must for you to do it
options.feedback: 'It is a must' is spoken register and does not appear in formal written English.

questions.explanation:
Modals of possibility are how English makes a request polite. A modal of obligation in the request would defeat its purpose.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence correctly states the reason for a request?
questions.context: A student explains to a school why a timetable change is needed.

options.text: I am writing because of clash my work.
options.feedback: 'Because of' is followed by a noun, not by a clause with a verb.

options.text: I am writing because my current timetable clashes with my part-time work.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Because' is followed by a complete clause with a subject, a verb and an object.

options.text: I am writing because my work clash.
options.feedback: A clause after 'because' needs a subject, and this one has none.

options.text: I am writing because of my work is clashing.
options.feedback: 'Because of' cannot be followed by a clause, so the structure is not possible.

questions.explanation:
'Because' introduces a clause and 'because of' introduces a noun phrase. Using the wrong one makes the sentence ungrammatical.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which phrase is suitable for asking the reader to reply in a formal email?
questions.context: A student asks a school office to acknowledge an email.

options.text: Reply fast please.
options.feedback: 'Reply fast please' is a spoken-style request that is too informal for a formal email.

options.text: Answer me soon.
options.feedback: 'Answer me soon' is a direct order in tone and does not suit the register.

options.text: I would be grateful for a response at your earliest convenience.
options.feedback: Correct! The hedged construction asks for a reply without imposing a deadline on the recipient.

options.text: You must reply now.
options.feedback: 'You must reply now' imposes an obligation and is not a request at all.

questions.explanation:
Hedged requests in English use 'would', 'grateful' and modal verbs. A polite email asks rather than instructs.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence correctly acknowledges information received?
questions.context: A student replies to a message already received and refers to it in the answer.

options.text: Thanks for the mail.
options.feedback: 'Thanks for the mail' is informal and calls an email a letter in a casual way.

options.text: I got your message, ok?
options.feedback: 'Ok' is spoken register and does not belong in a formal email.

options.text: You sent me an email before.
options.feedback: The last sentence states the fact without thanking the sender for it.

options.text: Thank you for your email of 3 May.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Thank you for' plus a precise reference to the date is the formal way of acknowledging a message.

questions.explanation:
Giving the date of the message you are answering is standard practice in formal correspondence and helps the reader find the earlier email.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence is appropriate for ending a request that asks the reader to do something?
questions.context: A student closes an email that asks a school to take a decision.

options.text: I look forward to hearing from you.
options.feedback: Correct! 'I look forward to hearing from you' is a standard formal way of closing a message that expects a reply.

options.text: Write me soon, ok?
options.feedback: 'Write me soon' is a spoken-style order, not a formal closing.

options.text: Waiting for your answer.
options.feedback: 'Waiting for your answer' states a fact in a way that reads as impatience.

options.text: You know what to do.
options.feedback: 'You know what to do' is informal and slightly rude in a request to a superior.

questions.explanation:
A formal closing sentence keeps the register consistent and signals politely that the writer is waiting for a response.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which element is NOT part of the layout of a formal email?
questions.context: A student checks the standard layout of a formal email before sending it.

options.text: The recipient's name in the opening line
options.feedback: The recipient's name in the opening line is part of the standard layout.

options.text: A signature written in capitals with the word 'bye'
options.feedback: Correct! 'Bye' is informal and does not belong in the signature block of a formal email.

options.text: A subject line above the greeting
options.feedback: The subject line belongs above the greeting.

options.text: A closing phrase before the signature
options.feedback: The closing phrase belongs before the signature.

questions.explanation:
Layout is part of the register. A correct structure with an informal word in it still reads as an informal message.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which verb is the most formal for requesting information in a letter?
questions.context: A student chooses the verb of the request in a letter to an institution.

options.text: ask
options.feedback: 'Ask' is neutral and would not by itself mark the message as formal.

options.text: check
options.feedback: 'Check' is a spoken expression rather than the verb of a formal request.

options.text: inquire
options.feedback: Correct! 'Inquire' is the formal verb used in written correspondence to request information.

options.text: find out
options.feedback: 'Find out' is a phrasal verb of neutral or informal register, not the verb of a formal letter.

questions.explanation:
A single verb can carry the register. Choosing 'inquire' rather than 'ask' signals formality without adding words.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence is written in the passive voice and suitable for a formal report?
questions.context: An office reports a completed administrative step in a formal document.

options.text: We received the documents on time.
options.feedback: The first sentence is active and names the agent, which a formal report often avoids.

options.text: The documents receive on time.
options.feedback: 'Receive' is a base form and cannot form a passive clause on its own.

options.text: The documents receiving on time.
options.feedback: 'Receiving' is a participle and cannot serve as the verb of a finite passive clause.

options.text: The documents were received on time.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Were received' is the past simple passive, which focuses on the action rather than on the agent.

questions.explanation:
Formal reports often use the passive to keep the process in the foreground and the person performing it in the background.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which phrase avoids direct criticism of a third person in a formal email?
questions.context: A student has to explain an absence in a message to a teacher or a principal.

options.text: I was unable to attend the meeting as it had been scheduled earlier.
options.feedback: Correct! The sentence states the fact and the circumstance without accusing anybody of a mistake.

options.text: I did not come because the meeting was badly scheduled.
options.feedback: The second sentence blames the person who set the meeting and is not appropriate in a formal message.

options.text: The meeting was scheduled badly, so I skipped it.
options.feedback: The third sentence names a fault directly and uses informal wording.

options.text: I could not go, the meeting was at a terrible time.
options.feedback: The last sentence is a spoken complaint with a subjective adjective.

questions.explanation:
Formal correspondence reports a circumstance rather than judging a person. Neutral wording protects the relationship and the writer.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence is the best way to give a reason for a late reply?
questions.context: A student answers an email several days after receiving it.

options.text: Sorry, was busy, no time.
options.feedback: The first sentence is spoken register and gives no reason.

options.text: I apologise for the delay in replying; I was away from school last week.
options.feedback: Correct! The sentence apologises formally and gives a clear, verifiable reason.

options.text: I was busy so I did not answer.
options.feedback: The third sentence blames the student rather than explaining the situation.

options.text: I had no time, that is why.
options.feedback: The last sentence is informal and does not apologise at all.

questions.explanation:
A short apology followed by a factual reason is the standard way of handling a late reply in a formal exchange.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which connector is most appropriate when adding a request to an existing explanation?
questions.context: A student writes to a school office and needs to add a second request to an explanation already given.

options.text: Anyway
options.feedback: 'Anyway' is a spoken discourse marker and is not used in a formal message.

options.text: So whatever
options.feedback: 'So whatever' is a spoken phrase that closes a discussion rather than adding to it.

options.text: In addition
options.feedback: Correct! 'In addition' formally introduces a further point in an explanation.

options.text: Well
options.feedback: 'Well' is a conversational filler and has no place in a formal email.

questions.explanation:
The connective has to match the register as well as the relationship between the ideas.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which structure is used to state a condition politely in a formal request?
questions.context: A student makes a request that depends on a decision taken by someone else.

options.text: If it is possible give it to me.
options.feedback: The first sentence is an order written without articles or capital letters.

options.text: If possible, give me the paper.
options.feedback: The second sentence drops the article and turns the request into a command.

options.text: If can be, approve this.
options.feedback: The third sentence is not a grammatical English structure.

options.text: If this is possible, I would be grateful for your approval.
options.feedback: Correct! The conditional structure defers to the recipient and the hedged second clause makes the request polite.

questions.explanation:
A condition plus a hedged main clause is one of the standard polite patterns of written English.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence uses a formal expression of regret correctly?
questions.context: An institution notifies a candidate of an unsuccessful application.

options.text: I regret to inform you that the application was not accepted.
options.feedback: Correct! 'I regret to inform you that' is a fixed formal expression used to deliver unwelcome news.

options.text: I regret say you no.
options.feedback: The second sentence omits the infinitive and the articles.

options.text: Sorry, no, you not accept.
options.feedback: The third sentence lacks the articles and the auxiliary and is not written English.

options.text: I am sad that maybe not accept the application.
options.feedback: The fourth sentence uses 'maybe' and a passive with a bare infinitive, which is not correct.

questions.explanation:
Formal English uses fixed expressions to soften bad news. Inventing a new wording of that kind produces a less appropriate register.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which attachment sentence is correct in a formal email?
questions.context: A student sends a document together with a message to a school office.

options.text: I put the certificate, you see it attached.
options.feedback: The first sentence is spoken register and does not name the attachment properly.

options.text: Please find attached the certificate of participation.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Please find attached' is the standard formula used to refer to a document sent with a formal message.

options.text: Attached is the certificate, look it.
options.feedback: The third sentence is a spoken instruction rather than a formal reference.

options.text: The certificate is attach, check it.
options.feedback: The fourth sentence uses a verb form that is not correct and an imperative without a subject.

questions.explanation:
Referring to an attachment is a fixed part of formal correspondence, and the formula carries the politeness of the message.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which email would be most appropriate for reporting a problem in a school laboratory?
questions.context: A student must report a laboratory fault to the person in charge in writing.

options.text: Subject: help. hi the sink is broke again, can u fix it tmrw?
options.feedback: The first message has no capitalisation, abbreviations and a chatty request.

options.text: Subject: Sink. It does not work. Fix it.
options.feedback: The second message is an order without articles and without any politeness.

options.text: Subject: Lab 3 sink not working. Dear Ms Ordonez, I am writing to report that the sink in laboratory 3 is not draining properly. Yours sincerely, Luis Vega
options.feedback: Correct! The message has a precise subject, a formal greeting, a factual report and a formal closing.

options.text: Subject: Laboratory. There is a sink. It has a problem.
options.feedback: The fourth message states the problem so vaguely that the reader cannot act on it.

questions.explanation:
A formal complaint about a facility needs four things: a clear subject, a polite opening, a factual description and a formal closing.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence states a purpose correctly in a formal email?
questions.context: A student writes to a school office to confirm an arrangement already agreed.

options.text: I am write for confirm the date.
options.feedback: 'Am write' is not a possible form of the verb 'be' with a gerund complement.

options.text: I am writing for to confirm the date.
options.feedback: 'For to confirm' places a preposition and an infinitive marker together, which is not a possible structure.

options.text: I am writing the date confirm.
options.feedback: 'Writing the date confirm' has no infinitive and does not express a purpose.

options.text: I am writing to confirm the date of the appointment.
options.feedback: Correct! 'I am writing to' is the standard formula for stating the aim of a formal message.

questions.explanation:
Stating the purpose of a message is one of the first duties of a formal letter, and English has a fixed formula for it.
---
questions.subject: ingles
